item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
232 did, however, hold that rating at one point in time, unless I'm much mistaken.

I'm not arguing its merits as an entry, merely its historical value - it was number 2, after all. 232 was brief and left a lot unsaid, very different to the modern style of SCP. I'm not surprised it therefore dropped in the ratings and got replaced. But if it hadn't remained protected, I suspect 173 would itself have been subject to expansion and modification, for similar reasons.

Am I the only one who thinks there's value in keeping a record of the original Keter object around? It needn't replace the current 232. SCPs have changed a great deal in style and new entries can only be compared to their contemporaries rather than the "original mould".

If this is a serious question, then you could answer it with a bare minimum amount of research (like reading the respective Wikipedia pages). Buck Rogers was the protagonist of "Armageddon 2419 AD" by Philip Francis Nolan in the August 1928 issue of Amazing Stories. The story was very popular and spun off a newspaper comic strip. In 1934, the Flash Gordon strip was created in order to capitalize on the same readership.

Buck is probably best known now for the 1979 TV show with Gil Gerard. Flash is probably best known for the Queen theme to the 1980 film.

item.content:encoded:
They've certainly benefited from copyright extensions on this one, yes. Had the copyright system not been revamped in the '70s, the first Jack Proton books would have started entering the public domain in 1996. Under the current copyright scheme, the books will become public domain in 2043, 70 years after Snyder's death, while the spinoff media (having been created by a corporation) will become public domain 95 years after creation, occurring gradually from 2042-2051.

Of course, it's not the media itself that's anomalous, it only causes problems if someone who's familiar with it should acquire one of the anomalous toys. By 2043, the toys will be close to 100 years old and it's likely that there will be very few left "in the wild" that are still functional.

The copyright, publication, and merchandising rights of the Jack Proton novels and all spinoff media are to be held by Springfield Crown Publishing, a Foundation front company, for the purpose of keeping the works out of print,

So maybe the Foundation is behind the ever repeating extensions to the length of copyright, so that anomalous copyrighted material never falls into the public domain?

item.content:encoded:
That's a really good point. What did sci-fi authors in that period do, normally? From memory, I can't remember race coming into any early Harry Harrison or even much in Ray Bradbury books, and it's not like either of them were exactly segregationists. And I can't remember any that feature space segregation explicitly, even if they. But I'm not from the US, and I'd live to hear other people's thoughts.

Realistically Snyder could just have sidestepped the issue by not having any black people, or not mentioning race at all. After all, all the names are futuristic, so there's way of denoting people as black without actually explicitly describing people or putting in stereotypical mannerisms.

You know, considering that these Jack Proton stories were first written back when xenophobic attitudes were the norm, I was half-expecting a black D-Class to be turned into some cringe-worthy Stepin Fetchit caricature who was happy to work under the boot of the main white characters, as a result of M. K. Snyder's racism and his assumption that segregation would be around all the way into the 27th century.

Alternatively, if the black D-Class character got to read some slightly less insensitive Jack Proton works from the '60s or '70s, he might've turned into some Captain Ethnic type, the token black character whose whole character, style and abilities revolved around the fact that he was black and who'll be blasted if he lets anyone forget he's black (because it sure is swell and unusual to have all these black characters in works nowadays)!

Or perhaps Snyder had more progressive views on that front?

There's no way the Foundation can suppress knowledge of the books' existence entirely. They can't possibly track down every copy sitting on the shelf in a public library, or at a yard sale, or swap meet, or what have you. What they can do is keep the books out of print and buy up copies that might end up on Amazon or eBay or so forth.

Really, the main difficulty for long-term containment (assuming any of the vintage toys are still floating around in the wild by then) is going to come in 2043, when the copyrights on the books expire.

In-universe, it would probably make sense that the reader knows who Jack Proton is, much like it can be assumed that any of us know who Buck Rogers or Flash Gordon are.

In a real sense, Jack Proton is an entirely original character produced for the purposes of this article, so it wouldn't do to simply assume that the reader already understands who the character is and the zeitgeist which he is part of.

In either event, it would stand to reason that the author would feel it necessary to explain who Jack Proton is, because it's quite possible that the intended reader of this article didn't grow up reading pulp sci-fi of a type that's been out of vogue for decades.
